about: The scripted AI lesson for p5-elasticity (2026-11-28, Phase C, brief docs/briefs/2026-11-27-phase-c-physics.md): every word she sees is written here once and checked (tools/check-script.js, tools/review-lesson.js --script). The AI only marks her typed answers (choosing a branch written here), answers her own questions, and sorts her messages. It opens with two recall questions from p5-gravity.

keyPoints.heading: Changing shape: stretching, bending and compressing

steps.text: Welcome! This lesson is about stretching, squashing and bending things, and the energy a stretched spring stores.

steps.question: First, two quick questions from the last lesson. What is the weight of a 0.5 kg mass where g = 9.8 N/kg?

wrong.mass: Not quite: 0.5 kg is the mass. The weight is W = m g = 0.5 × 9.8 = 4.9 N.
wrong.divide: Not quite: multiply the mass by g: 0.5 × 9.8 = 4.9 N.

idk.hint: Weight = mass × g, where g is gravity's pull on each kilogram: here 9.8 N/kg.

steps.question: Second: which force keeps a satellite in its orbit?
steps.right: Yes: gravity pulls the satellite towards the Earth and keeps it going round.

wrong.air: Not quite: there is almost no air up there. Gravity keeps it in orbit.
wrong.friction: Not quite: nothing rubs on a satellite. Gravity keeps it in orbit.

idk.hint: Which force pulls the satellite towards the Earth?

steps.answerWhy: Gravity pulls the satellite towards the Earth all the time, which keeps it going round in its orbit.

steps.text: Now this lesson. Forces can change the shape of an object. You can stretch it, as when you pull a spring; compress it, which means squash it, as when you sit on a cushion; or bend it, as a diver bends a diving board.
A still object needs more than one force on it before its shape can change. With only one force it would not stay still: it would move off in the direction of the force.

steps.question: A spring hangs from a clamp with masses on the end, and it is stretched. Which forces stretch it?

options.text: The masses pulling down and the clamp pulling up

steps.right: Yes: it takes two forces, one at each end, to stretch a spring that is not moving.

wrong.other: Not quite: the masses pulling down and the clamp pulling up.
wrong.masses: Not quite: with only the masses pulling, the spring would fall. The clamp pulls up too, and the two forces stretch it.
wrong.clamp: Not quite: one force alone would just move the spring. The masses pull down and the clamp pulls up: two forces at the two ends stretch it.

idk.hint: The masses pull down. Is anything pulling the other way at the top?

steps.answerWhy: The masses pull down and the clamp pulls up: two forces at the two ends stretch the still spring.

steps.text: Some objects go back to their first shape and length when the forces are removed. That kind of change of shape is called elastic deformation.
Other objects stay changed when the forces are removed: that is called inelastic deformation. The same spring can do both: elastic when stretched a little, inelastic when stretched too far.

steps.question: A plastic bag is stretched so much that it stays longer, even after you let go. What kind of deformation is that?
steps.right: Yes: it does not go back to its first shape, so it is inelastic deformation.

wrong.elastic: Not quite: elastic means it goes back to its first shape. The bag stays longer, so it is inelastic.
wrong.none: Not quite: its shape has changed, so it has deformed. It stays changed, so it is inelastic deformation.

idk.hint: Does the bag go back to its first shape when you let go?

steps.answerWhy: The bag stays longer when the force is removed, so it has deformed inelastically.

steps.prompt: In one line: what is the difference between elastic and inelastic deformation?
points: After elastic deformation, an object goes back to its first shape
After inelastic deformation, it stays changed
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: after elastic deformation an object goes back to its first shape, but after inelastic deformation it stays changed.

steps.text: When you stretch a spring, it gets longer. How much longer it gets is called the extension: stretched length minus original length.

steps.question: A spring is 20 cm long. With a mass hung on it, it is 26 cm long. What is the extension, in cm?

wrong.other: Not quite: 6 cm. Extension = stretched length − original length = 26 − 20 = 6 cm.
wrong.length: Not quite: 26 cm is the stretched length. The extension is how much longer it got: 26 − 20 = 6 cm.
wrong.add: Not quite: take the original length away: 26 − 20 = 6 cm.

steps.text: Hang twice the weight on a spring and you get twice the extension. Extension is directly proportional to force.

steps.question: A spring stretches 2 cm with a force of 1 N. If it stays proportional, how far does it stretch with a force of 3 N, in cm?
steps.right: Yes: three times the force gives three times the extension: 3 × 2 = 6 cm.

wrong.other: Not quite: 6 cm. Three times the force gives three times the extension: 3 × 2 = 6 cm.
wrong.add: Not quite: 6 cm. Proportional means multiply, not add: three times the force gives 3 × 2 = 6 cm.
wrong.add2: Not quite: 6 cm. Proportional means multiply: three times the force gives 3 × 2 = 6 cm.

idk.hint: 3 N is three times 1 N. What happens to the extension?

steps.answerWhy: 3 N is three times 1 N, so the extension is three times 2 cm: 6 cm.

steps.text: Proportionality holds only up to a point. Stretched further, the spring stops following the rule. The point where it stops is called the limit of proportionality.
Each spring has its own spring constant, k: how stiff it is. A stiff spring has a big spring constant: it needs a big force to stretch it a little.
The equation linking force, spring constant and extension is F = k e. F is in newtons (N) and e in metres (m). k is in newtons per metre (N/m): the force needed for each metre of extension.
Here is a worked example. Tap "Show the first step" under it to see each step in turn.
steps.question: A force of 4 N stretches a spring by 0.08 m. What is its spring constant?
steps: Write the equation: F = k e.
Divide both sides by e: k = F ÷ e.

steps.question: Your turn. A force of 6 N stretches a spring by 3 cm. What is its spring constant, in N/m? (100 cm = 1 m.)

wrong.other: Not quite: 200 N/m. 3 cm = 0.03 m, and k = F ÷ e = 6 ÷ 0.03 = 200 N/m.
wrong.cm: Not quite: 200 N/m. Change centimetres to metres first: 3 cm = 0.03 m. Then 6 ÷ 0.03 = 200 N/m.
wrong.times: Not quite: 200 N/m. Divide the force by the extension: 6 ÷ 0.03 = 200 N/m.
wrong.flip: Not quite: 200 N/m. Divide the force by the extension, not the other way round: 6 ÷ 0.03 = 200 N/m.

idk.hint: Change 3 cm into metres first: 100 cm = 1 m. Then k = F ÷ e.

steps.text: F = k e also works for squashing. Then e is how much shorter the object gets, called its compression.

steps.prompt: In one line: what does F = k e tell you about a spring?
points: The extension is proportional to the force
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: for a spring, force = spring constant × extension, so the extension is proportional to the force up to the limit of proportionality.

steps.question: Before a practical with springs: to find a spring's extension, what must you measure?

options.text: Its original length and its stretched length

steps.right: Yes: extension = stretched length − original length, so you need both.

wrong.other: Not quite: its original length and its stretched length.
wrong.stretched: Not quite: the stretched length alone is not the extension. You also need the original length to take away.
wrong.mass: Not quite: the spring's own mass does not give the extension. You need the original and stretched lengths.

steps.answerWhy: Extension = stretched length − original length, so you must measure both lengths.

steps.text: In a class practical, you hang a spring from a clamp with a ruler beside it. You measure its original length, then add masses one at a time and measure the stretched length each time.
The force on the spring is the weight of the hanging masses: W = m g, weight (N) = mass (kg) × g (N/kg).

steps.question: How should you read the ruler to measure the spring's length accurately?

options.text: With your eye level with the bottom of the spring
From above, looking down the spring
From below, looking up at it

steps.right: Yes: with your eye level with the bottom of the spring, you do not read the ruler too high or too low.

wrong.other: Not quite: with your eye level with the bottom of the spring.
wrong.above: Not quite: from above, the mark you line up with looks lower or higher than it really is. Keep your eye level with the bottom of the spring.
wrong.below: Not quite: from below, the mark you line up with looks higher or lower than it really is. Keep your eye level with the bottom of the spring.

idk.hint: Reading a scale at an angle gives the wrong value. Where should your eye be?

steps.answerWhy: Reading with your eye level with the bottom of the spring stops you reading the ruler too high or too low.

steps.text: The results go on a graph, with force up the side and extension along the bottom.
The origin is the corner of the graph where both force and extension are zero.
A graph that is a straight line shows a linear relationship. For a spring the line also goes through the origin, so force and extension are directly proportional.

steps.question: On a force-extension graph, the line is straight at first, then starts to curve. What do you think the curve shows?

options.text: The limit of proportionality has been passed
No more force is being added

steps.right: Yes: after the limit of proportionality, extension is no longer proportional to force, so the line curves.

wrong.other: Not quite: the limit of proportionality has been passed.
wrong.stiffer: Not quite: a stiffer spring needs more force for each centimetre, which would make a straight line steeper, not curved. A curve means the limit of proportionality has been passed.
wrong.noforce: Not quite: the force up the side keeps rising as masses are added. The curve shows the limit of proportionality has been passed.

idk.hint: Up to which point is extension proportional to force?

steps.answerWhy: The line curves once the limit of proportionality is passed, because extension is then no longer proportional to force.

steps.text: A relationship with a curved graph is called a non-linear relationship.
The gradient is how steep the line is. On the straight part, the gradient of the force-extension graph is the spring constant: the change in force ÷ the change in extension.

steps.question: Between two points on the straight part, the force goes up by 10 N and the extension by 0.25 m. What is the spring constant, in N/m?

wrong.other: Not quite: 40 N/m. Gradient = rise in force ÷ rise in extension = 10 ÷ 0.25 = 40 N/m.
wrong.times: Not quite: 40 N/m. Divide the force by the extension: 10 ÷ 0.25 = 40 N/m.
wrong.flip: Not quite: 40 N/m. Divide the force by the extension, not the other way round: 10 ÷ 0.25 = 40 N/m.

idk.hint: The gradient is the change in force divided by the change in extension: 10 ÷ 0.25.

steps.answerWhy: The gradient is 10 ÷ 0.25 = 40, so k = 40 N/m.

steps.prompt: In one line: what does a straight line through the origin on a force-extension graph show?
points: It shows that force and extension are directly proportional
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: a straight line through the origin on a force-extension graph shows that force and extension are directly proportional; its gradient is the spring constant.

keyPoints.heading: Work done and elastic potential energy

steps.text: When a force moves something, it does work: it transfers energy. Stretching a spring takes work, because your force moves through a distance.
Energy stored in a stretched or squashed object is called elastic potential energy.
If the spring goes back to its original shape afterwards, all the work done on it is stored. Let go, and it can give that energy back.
The equation is Ee = ½ k e²: elastic potential energy = 0.5 × spring constant × extension squared. Ee is in joules (J), k in N/m and e in metres (m). It works up to the limit of proportionality.
Here is a worked example. Tap "Show the first step" under it to see each step in turn.
steps.question: A spring with k = 50 N/m is stretched by 0.08 m. How much elastic potential energy does it store?
steps: Write the equation: Ee = ½ k e².

steps.question: Your turn. A spring with k = 200 N/m is stretched by 0.1 m. How much elastic potential energy does it store, in J?

wrong.nosquare: Not quite: 1 J. Square the extension: 0.1² = 0.01. Then 0.5 × 200 × 0.01 = 1 J.
wrong.nohalf: Not quite: 1 J. Remember the ½: 0.5 × 200 × 0.01 = 1 J.
wrong.neither: Not quite: 1 J. Square the extension and take half: 0.5 × 200 × 0.1² = 1 J.

idk.hint: Square 0.1 first, then multiply by 200 and by 0.5.

steps.question: A spring with k = 400 N/m is stretched by 5 cm. How much energy does it store, in J?

wrong.cm: Not quite: 0.5 J. Change 5 cm to 0.05 m first. Then 0.5 × 400 × 0.05² = 0.5 J.
wrong.nosquare: Not quite: 0.5 J. Square the extension: 0.05² = 0.0025. Then 0.5 × 400 × 0.0025 = 0.5 J.

idk.hint: Change 5 cm into metres, square it, then multiply by 400 and by 0.5.

steps.prompt: In one line: what is elastic potential energy, and how do you work it out?
points: It is energy stored in a stretched or squashed object
It is worked out with Ee = ½ k e²
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: elastic potential energy is the energy stored in a stretched or squashed object: Ee = ½ k e².

steps.text: Now for a short quiz: six questions on the whole lesson. Take your time.

steps.question: Quiz, question 1 of 6: a spring goes back to its first length when the masses are taken off. What kind of deformation was it?
steps.right: Yes: it went back to its first shape, so the deformation was elastic.

wrong.inelastic: Not quite: inelastic means it stays changed. This spring went back, so it was elastic.
wrong.nonlinear: Not quite: non-linear describes a graph. Going back to its first shape is elastic deformation.

idk.hint: Did the spring go back to its first shape?

steps.answerWhy: The spring went back to its first shape when the force was removed, so the deformation was elastic.

steps.question: Quiz, question 2 of 6: a spring 15 cm long is stretched to 23 cm. What is its extension?

wrong.length: Not quite: 23 cm is the stretched length. The extension is 23 − 15 = 8 cm.
wrong.add: Not quite: subtract the original length: 23 − 15 = 8 cm.

steps.question: Quiz, question 3 of 6: a force of 10 N gives an extension of 0.5 m. What is the spring constant?

wrong.times: Not quite: divide the force by the extension: 10 ÷ 0.5 = 20 N/m.
wrong.flip: Not quite: divide the force by the extension: 10 ÷ 0.5 = 20 N/m.

steps.question: Quiz, question 4 of 6: what does the gradient of the straight part of a force-extension graph give?
steps.right: Yes: force ÷ extension is the spring constant.

wrong.extension: Not quite: the extension is along the bottom. The gradient, force ÷ extension, is the spring constant.
wrong.energy: Not quite: the gradient is force ÷ extension, which is the spring constant.

idk.hint: The gradient is the rise in force ÷ the rise in extension.

steps.answerWhy: The gradient is force ÷ extension, which is the spring constant k.

steps.question: Quiz, question 5 of 6: what does a graph of a non-linear relationship look like?

options.text: A straight line through the origin

steps.right: Yes: a non-linear relationship gives a curve.

wrong.straight: Not quite: a straight line shows a linear relationship. Non-linear gives a curve.
wrong.flat: Not quite: a flat line is still straight, so it would be linear. A non-linear relationship gives a curve.

idk.hint: Linear means straight. What is the opposite?

steps.answerWhy: A non-linear relationship gives a curved graph.

steps.question: Quiz, question 6 of 6: a spring with k = 100 N/m is stretched by 0.2 m. How much energy does it store?

wrong.nosquare: Not quite: square the extension: 0.2² = 0.04. Then 0.5 × 100 × 0.04 = 2 J.
wrong.nohalf: Not quite: remember the ½: 0.5 × 100 × 0.04 = 2 J.

steps.text: That's the end of the quiz: you got {right} out of {n}.

end.text: The lesson is finished. Tap a button to go on.
